title: K1-K3 ciphertext-invariant mining (family-matched nulls) -> forward filter
hypothesis: a higher-order ciphertext statistic shared by the known K1-K3 (beyond their cipher family) acts as a new forward constraint K4 must match
best_partial: 0 strict K1-K3 invariants (MC chance 0.048); K2+K3 share 0, K4 aligns on 0 (incl. doublet-rate trend)
insights: Computed 10 length-robust ciphertext-only stats on K1-K4, z-scored each section against a FAMILY-MATCHED null (K1/K2 vs Quagmire-III, K3 vs columnar, K4 vs both; 300 samples each). This removes the cipher-type artifact that an earlier substitution-only null produced on K3.

STRICT shared K1-K3 invariants (all three deviate same-sign, |z|>1 vs own-family null): NONE. Monte-Carlo chance rate for finding >=1 such stat under the matched nulls = 0.048 (1500 trials). Within chance noise -- no robust all-three invariant.

LESS-RIGID view (K2+K3, the long cipher-comparable sections): same-sign |z|>1 on NONE; of these K4 ALIGNS on none. Doublet-rate z (the trend an earlier rigid gate hid): K1=-0.87, K2=1.68, K3=-0.62, K4(sub)=1.05, K4(col)=0.15.

VERDICT: no shared K1-K3 ciphertext invariant clears the Monte-Carlo chance bar under family-matched nulls -- no new hard forward filter on K4. This is specific to these statistics and the all-of-K1-K3 rule, not a proof that K4's higher-order structure is featureless.
next_steps: no hard forward invariant; the soft K2/K3/K4 doublet trend is a weak hint, not a constraint. The per-position frame stays bounded for short rules; the residue is idiosyncratic -- next is a structural/writeup decision, not another single-cipher KPA
